The potential edge is plausible because legislative, lobbying, trading, news, and social data can reveal information before it is fully incorporated into prices, but the same data are noisy, delayed, incomplete, and difficult to translate into causal predictions. The committee should therefore ask the manager to demonstrate incremental out-of-sample returns from each signal family separately, rather than accepting a blended backtest whose strongest results may come from one unstable or accidentally leaked feature.

Ask for a complete signal dictionary showing each data source, collection time, publication time, licensing terms, revisions, missingness, geographic and political coverage, and the exact timestamp at which the strategy could legitimately have acted.

Lobbying data deserve particular skepticism because disclosure rules differ across jurisdictions, informal or private influence may be absent, and the observed relationship between lobbying activity and policy outcomes is confounded by many other factors. [shard_01349_63235]

For congressional trades, ask whether the system uses legally public filings or obtains tips, embargoed feeds, personal data, hacked material, or information supplied under confidentiality, and require written counsel’s analysis of insider-trading, misappropriation, confidentiality, privacy, and data-licensing risks.

The STOCK Act increased public reporting of congressional transactions above $1,000 to within 45 days, but public disclosure does not by itself prove that a trade is lawful, timely enough to monetize, or free of an appearance-of-conflict problem. [shard_05753_35573]

Ask whether the manager has controls preventing the strategy from trading on material nonpublic information, whether every source is archived with its access conditions, and whether compliance can reconstruct the information available before every order.

Ask how the strategy handles social-media impersonation, bots, coordinated campaigns, deleted posts, satire, translation errors, hacked accounts, and synthetic or AI-generated content, because a fake social-media message has previously produced an almost immediate market decline followed by a recovery. [shard_03450_62513]

Require an independent data-quality study measuring precision, recall, duplicate content, survivorship bias, timestamp accuracy, revisions, source concentration, and the performance impact of removing the most questionable sources.

Ask the manager to distinguish prediction from explanation: a model may identify correlations in text without establishing that a bill, lobbyist, headline, or geopolitical event caused the market move, and apparent confidence scores must be calibrated against realized outcomes rather than treated as probabilities by assertion. [shard_00925_25381] [shard_03434_14812]

Demand a model inventory covering every classifier, language model, ranking system, portfolio optimizer, execution algorithm, and vendor model, together with ownership, version history, training data, validation results, known failure modes, and change-approval procedures.

Require genuinely out-of-sample and walk-forward testing with point-in-time data, realistic publication and execution delays, transaction costs, spreads, market impact, borrow costs, capacity limits, and a documented prohibition on tuning the strategy to the test period.

Curve-fitting and dependence on accurate, timely data are recognized automated-trading risks, so the manager should show performance across political administrations, election cycles, wars, volatility regimes, liquidity conditions, and periods in which the relevant signal was widely known. Ask what happens when models disagree, confidence collapses, a data feed stops, a source changes its format, a vendor is compromised, or an event moves prices faster than the system can validate it.
